summary.text: 告 is used to tell, report, announce, inform, and accuse. Its construction is disputed: one proposal sees an open mouth with a protruding tongue, while others analyze 口 with an upper element identified as 牛 or abbreviated 壴.

formation.text: The graph is analyzed either as an open mouth with a protruding tongue or as 口 combined with an upper element identified as 牛 or abbreviated 壴. The identity and function of that upper element remain uncertain.

components.text: In the mouth-and-tongue proposal, 口 depicts an open mouth. It also appears in the 牛-plus-mouth and 壴-plus-mouth analyses, though those proposals do not specify a separate function for it.

history.text: The Shuowen account interprets 告 as an ox striking a person while a crossbar restrains its horns, thereby informing people, and analyzes the graph as 牛 plus 口. A later account describes the seal form changing through clerical abbreviation and regular-script shaping into the modern form; this does not confirm the earlier graph’s parts.
Uses are reported in oracle-bone, Western Zhou bronze, and Warring States materials, but the cited examples establish neither a sequence of graphic forms nor a chronology of meanings.

uncertainties.text: The mouth-and-tongue, 牛-plus-mouth, and 壴-plus-mouth analyses compete; the early upper element is not securely identified.

A Southwestern Mandarin word meaning “try” or “check out” is proposed to have been written with 告 by reusing the graph for 校. The reported Middle Chinese readings are similar, but the direction and sound pathway of the borrowing remain uncertain.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone and later examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone example concerning a deer report and later reporting or telling uses are cited. These attest such uses but do not establish one original meaning or a sequence of semantic change.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Western Zhou bronze examples include reporting and admonishing uses. They do not establish when these uses arose or how they relate chronologically to earlier ones.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Accusatory use is reported among Western Zhou bronze examples; its relationship to “report” is not established.
Modern uses include telling, announcing, informing, and accusing. Their listing does not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

A Southwestern Mandarin word meaning “try” or “check out” is attested in a 1909 example. 告 is proposed to reuse the graph for 校 to write this similar-sounding word; the borrowing direction and sound pathway remain uncertain. This is not evidence that “tell” developed into “try”.

limitations.text: The cited examples do not establish a sequence connecting sacrificial, reporting, admonishing, accusatory, and telling uses.
The proposed borrowing from 校 lacks independent confirmation of its source account and historical sound pathway; similarity alone does not establish the borrowing direction.
